AI careers

Your first AI portfolio needs a useful problem, not another impressive demo.

Build a small enquiry-drafting project with fictional information, a clear test record and an honest account of what you contributed.

Anzolo Kpazhi Hope19 November 2026 · 5 min read

You have watched the tutorials. You can write a prompt and get a polished answer. But when someone asks what you can actually do with AI, you struggle to show them something that is yours. If you are starting your career in Nigeria or elsewhere in Africa with limited money and data, that gap can feel expensive to close.

I would start with one small project you can explain from beginning to end. You do not need to buy a subscription or pretend you have a client. You need a recognisable problem, a working example and evidence of the decisions you made. Let me walk you through a project you can build around a fictional tutoring centre.

Give your project one person to serve

Imagine an administrator answering repeated questions about lesson times, fees and enrolment. This is a fictional practice scenario, not a report about any school I work with. Your task is to help that administrator prepare a reply from a short information sheet. The administrator still checks and sends it.

Write a one-sentence brief: “I am building a draft-reply workflow that uses the centre’s approved information and flags questions that need a person.” Keep admissions decisions, payment verification and messages to real families outside the project. A narrow brief gives you something you can actually finish.

Create the evidence before the answer

Make a fictional information sheet with two courses, lesson times, fees, an update date and a contact route. Label it “fictional demonstration data”. Include a rule that places and special arrangements must be confirmed by the administrator. Use no real student names, phone numbers, messages or records.

Next, write ten imaginary enquiries. Include straightforward questions, one asking for an unlisted course, one asking for a discount and one with an unclear lesson time. For each enquiry, write the facts a correct reply should contain and anything it must leave for clarification. Do this before running the AI. Otherwise, an attractive answer can quietly change what you count as correct.

Build a modest version you can inspect

Use a document or spreadsheet for the information sheet and test log. If you already have access to a free AI tool, provide only the fictional sheet and one enquiry at a time. Ask it to draft a short response using that sheet, flag missing information and identify which facts it used. You do not need an API or an automated messaging connection for this exercise.

If you code, a small interface can make the demonstration easier to follow. If you do not, a carefully documented manual workflow is a valid learning project. Name it accurately: an AI-assisted drafting workflow, not an autonomous school-management system. If tool access is unavailable, prepare the materials offline and label the AI execution as pending rather than presenting invented outputs.

Keep the corrections in your portfolio

For each case, record the input, expected facts, actual draft, corrections and your final judgement. Check whether the reply preserved the course and fee, avoided unsupported promises and asked for clarification when needed. A single invented discount should remain visible even if the other replies read beautifully.

Use five enquiries while improving your instructions, then try the other five without tailoring the instructions to their answers. Keep both sets of results. This small exercise can reveal weaknesses; it cannot establish general accuracy or production readiness. If you repeat a run, record the new result rather than replacing the awkward one. Note the tool, displayed model name if available, and test date so the limits of your evidence are clear.

Make your own contribution easy to see

Prepare a short case study with the problem, fictional information sheet, instructions, test log, one failed output and the correction you made. Explain why a human reviews the draft and what you would need to investigate before using real enquiries. Include screenshots or saved text so someone can understand the project without a live demonstration.

Write a precise contribution statement: “I defined the task, created the fictional test cases, checked the drafts and documented the failure cases. AI generated the draft responses.” If AI also helped with code or documentation, say where. This gives a reader a clearer basis for assessing your work than a broad claim that you built an intelligent assistant.

UNESCO’s 2024 AI competency framework for students describes progression through understanding, application and creation, alongside attention to people, ethics, techniques and system design. It is an education framework, not a recruitment standard. My portfolio exercise is an independent practical suggestion: show how you think and test, as well as what a tool produces.

Finish one useful example before expanding

This connects to the education and practical adoption direction of my work through ECHUKU. I want learning to leave you able to explain a problem, make a sensible design choice and recognise a result that needs correction. The earlier THISDAY feature linked below records a different period of my work; it does not evaluate or endorse this exercise.

Give yourself three short working sessions: one to define the task and examples, one to build and test, and one to write up what happened. You can show the result to a trusted peer using only the fictional materials. Ask them what they cannot understand without your explanation, then improve that part.

A small portfolio project does not guarantee a job or prove that you are ready for every AI role. It does give you a concrete piece of work to discuss and a clearer view of what to learn next. If you need help choosing that direction, start with my free AI Career Guide below and the invitation to the free Anzolo Hope AI Fellowship community.
